title: Attention chain restart: sampler probes and restart impact
content:
Goal:
Quick investigation into an emergent p99/p999 latency pattern tied to repeated generation 'chain restarts' observed in customer traces. Hypothesis: stochastic sampler decisions cause micro restarts (partial KV resets / replay) and interact badly with our opportunistic kernel selection (FlashAttention vs paged-attn + fused ops toggles), producing kernel-handoff overheads and prefetch thrashing.

Background/context:
- "Chain restart" = request flow where generation is stopped and restarted with a new prompt/context overlap (common in multi-turn chat or when sampling/backtracking triggers re-encoding). Causes: tool-calling, stop-token handling, reinforcement sampling heuristics (top-p jitter).
- Production symptom: stable median latency but intermittent long tails (p99 -> p999 spikes) correlating to requests that do many short restarts (e.g., length cycles like 48 tokens + restart, repeated).

Environment / test harness:
- Hardware: NVIDIA A100-SXM 80GB, CUDA 12.1, cuDNN 9.x.
- Model: Llama-2-7B (FP16), Redwood serving runtime v0.46.2-dev.
- FlashAttention: v2.0.1 (patched), published paged-attn branch (internal patchset for page-size 128).
- Workload: synthetic replay of sampled customer traces with controlled restart frequency.
- Metrics tooling: per-token tracing enabled, kernel timeline via nvprof/NSight snapshot, host-side event tracing (tok_profiler), and runtime logs with kernel-choice events.

Experiment matrix (selected):
- restart-frequency: none (continuous), every 256 tokens, every 64 tokens, restart-on-every-sample (stress).
- batch: 1, 4, 16 (single-request hot path focused on batch=1).
- seq-lengths: context 512 / generate up to 1024, warm vs cold KV cache variants.
- fused_ops: on/off; opportunistic-kernel-switch: enabled/disabled.
- paged page_size: 128 (default patch) / 256.

Representative raw numbers (median/p95/p99 per-token latency, batch=1, 7B FP16):
- Baseline (continuous, no restarts, FA enabled, fused ops on): median 6.8ms token, p95 11.2ms, p99 18.4ms.
- Restart every 256 tokens: median 7.4ms (+9%), p99 24.5ms (+33%).
- Restart every 64 tokens: median 7.6ms (+12%), p95 18.8ms, p99 42.1ms (+128%).
- Aggressive restarts (every sample): median 9.1ms, p99 112ms (dominated by repeated kernel rebinds and host-side scheduling).
- Opportunistic kernel switch disabled (every-64 restarts): p99 improves to 28ms (suggests kernel switching amplifies tail).

Key traces & observed behaviors:
1) Kernel handoff count spikes on restart: requests that include a restart frequently trigger a different kernel path mid-request (FlashAttention -> paged-attn (fallback) or vice versa). We saw sequences where the runtime chooses FA for initial tokens but falls back to paged-attn when page boundary alignment shifts after restart. Each handoff adds 0.6–1.2ms of overhead (kernel teardown + prefetch adjustments).

2) Prefetch hysteresis / page boundary penalty: paged-attn prefetch logic is tuned for monotonic generation. When restarts cause the logical token index to jump backward/forward relative to page boundaries, the prefetcher issues extra DMA/prepare work. Measured additional GPU idle gaps of 0.9–2.1ms at page-alignment events. Page_size=256 reduced frequency of these events but increased average kernel memory footprint and sometimes higher median latency for long sequences.

3) KV reinit cost is non-trivial for small context restarts: when we discard and re-encode context (common in backtrack), KV allocation + initial KV kernel priming costs ~1.4–1.9ms on our stack. With many restarts this amortizes poorly. Keeping stale KV around (soft keepalive) reduced p99 significantly in stress runs.

4) Small-batch scheduling jitter: sampler micro-bursts create many short tasks that are scheduled on host side. Host-to-device enqueue jitter (0.5–1.0ms) multiplied by restart frequency explains part of the spike. Coalescing at the scheduler (microbatching of consecutive mini-restarts) reduced spikes in experiments.

Profiling snippets (representative):
- nvprof timeline: "flash_attn_kernel_v2" (12.2us kernels) interspersed with "paged_prefetch" gaps (1.2ms), "kv_init" host->device memcpy (0.9ms).
- runtime log lines: [2025-02-20T17:02:11Z] request=abc kernel_choice=FlashAttention sequence_index=64 kernel_switch=True fallback_reason=page-misalignment

Hypotheses (prioritized):
A. Opportunistic kernel switching across restarts creates extra overhead; the switch decisions are brittle at short sequence boundaries.
B. Paged-attn prefetch logic lacks resilience to sequence index discontinuities introduced by chain restarts and sampler backtracks.
C. KV lifecycle policy is too eager (free/realloc on restart) causing repeated priming costs.
D. Host scheduler microburst sensitivity magnifies kernel handoff overhead for batch=1 workloads.

Mitigations tried (quick experiments):
1) Disable opportunistic kernel switching for requests that have had a restart in the past N tokens (N=128): p99 reduced ~30% on restart-heavy traces.
2) Introduce a soft keepalive for KV buffers for 2x mean-restart-interval: p99 improved 40% in synthetic workload; memory overhead limited but needs safety checks.
3) Coalesce restarts at the scheduler by delaying the enqueue of tiny restarts by 0.8ms and merging if another arrive -> reduced host jitter but added small median penalty for isolated restarts. Net benefit for heavy-churn scenarios.
4) Page_size experiment: 128->256 reduced prefetch events but raised median for long sequences; suggests dynamic page sizing might be best.

Actionable recommendations (short-term):
- Ship nginx/route level flag to disable opportunistic kernel switching for small-batch interactive endpoints until we harden policy.
- Implement KV soft-keepalive (configurable TTL) behind a feature flag and run on Canary. Add guard to evict under memory pressure.
- Add metric: runtime.attn.kernel_handoffs and runtime.attn.restart_count per request to link tail events to handoffs.
- Add instrumentation to paged-attn prefetcher to record page-misalignment events and DMA counts.
- Scheduler: implement optional micro-coalescing window for enqueueing restart-driven short tasks.

Longer-term / research items:
- Explore a deterministic kernel affinity policy that is sticky per-request unless explicit compatibility reason to switch (instead of per-token heuristic).
- Consider a hybrid prefetch strategy: favor conservative prefetch around restart-prone offsets and aggressive prefetch for sustained monotonic streams.
- Evaluate model-level prompt stitching to avoid restarts where possible (application change).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What's the memory budget impact of KV soft-keepalive at 80–90th percentile traffic? Need capacity run.
- Is there any pathological combination of models (e.g., mixing 7B and 70B) that exacerbates handoffs due to variant-specific kernel choices?
- Can we get scheduler-level telemetry at the microsecond resolution in production without prohibitive cost?

Quick checklist for next week:
- [ ] Add kernel_handoffs metric & restart_count per request (owner: Lucas)
- [ ] PR: soft-keepalive for KV with eviction policy (owner: Priya)
- [ ] Canary: disable opportunistic-kernel-switch for interactive routes (owner: Evelyn)
- [ ] Run 24h replay of customer-trace A with new flags and capture p50/p95/p99 deltas (owner: Michael)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally exploratory: numbers vary by GPU and model size. Please run your own microbench against your hardware.
- We observed similar patterns on p4d and A100, though magnitudes differ (p4d had slightly worse enqueue jitter).

Appendix: quick commands used
- Generate replay workload: python infra/tools/replay_trace.py --trace traces/chat-heavy.json --rate 20 --restart-probability 0.35
- Capture kernel timeline (short): nsight-compute -f kernel.ncu --set full --target-processes all --trace ctrace -- python server/bin/serve --config test.yaml
- Dump runtime kernel-choice events: grep kernel_choice logs/*.log | sed -n '1,200p'

If you want raw traces (nvprof files, replay trace), leave a note and I'll attach to CONFLUENCE-ATTN-245.

-- Michael
